**Before the visit**
- Add the appointment date under the Visit tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what would make them stronger.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most. Stick to three or four.
- Make your notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the visit**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is made so it can be read in under a minute: counts, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can make the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

They are a summary of what you entered, plus what you yourself chose to pull from Apple Health. They are not a diagnosis or a complete medical record, and any patterns in them are coincidence checks, not proof of a cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the visit**

Add new medication with a start date. In a few weeks MenoMap can show your entries before and after, which makes your next follow-up easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day that marks 12 months in a row without a period, when it is not due to something else (such as pregnancy, certain medicines or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but anything from the mid 40s to the mid 50s is common.

**Perimenopause** is the years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, closer together or further apart. Many of the changes associated with the change of life, such as hot flashes, night sweats, changes in sleep and changes in mood, often begin here, while you still have periods. Perimenopause can last a few years or quite a lot longer, and it looks different for everyone.

**Postmenopause** is everything after the 12-month mark. Some symptoms fade over time; others can continue for years.

Menopause can also come earlier because of an operation in which the ovaries are removed, certain cancer treatments or other health conditions. Menopause before 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth talking to a doctor about.

**How it is established.** In many people over 45, the doctor can establish perimenopause or menopause from your medical history and your symptoms. Blood tests are not always necessary, because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. They are used more often when you are younger or when the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. But the app can keep an honest log of what you notice: waves, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, on the neck and chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, palpitations or a chill afterwards. Night sweats are the same during sleep, and it can be so heavy that you wake up or that your bedding gets soaked.

They are among the most common changes around the change of life. Some have few and mild ones; others have many a day, which disrupt work and sleep. For some they disappear within a few years; for others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** Many notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, warm rooms, stress or heavy bedding. It varies greatly from person to person, and therefore it can be more useful to follow your own tags than a general list.

**There are other causes.** Flushing and sweating can also be due to thyroid problems, infections, certain medicines, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or if they come together with weight loss, fever or a feeling of being ill, then mention it to a doctor.

**Describe them well.** Useful details for a visit:
- Roughly how many per day and per night
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to come before them
- What you have tried and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's Wave button and after-the-fact logging exist precisely to catch this without much trouble.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options as well as practical measures. Which ones suit you is a conversation to have with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces some of the estrogen the body produces less of around the change of life. Leading professional guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gel, spray, tablets and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as dryness. Those who still have a uterus are normally prescribed a progestogen together with the estrogen to protect the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on the individual:** age, how much time has passed since periods stopped, own and family medical history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease) and which type of treatment it is and how it is given. Therefore it is a decision to be made together with a doctor who knows your medical history, and not something an app can decide.

**Questions many ask:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- Which type and form would you suggest, and why?
- Which benefits can I expect, and how quickly?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare with not being treated?
- What should I watch for, and when should we follow up?

**If you already receive it,** then record it in MenoMap (You → Medication). MenoMap shows your waves before and after you began, as a coincidence check and not proof, so that you have something concrete to talk about at the follow-up.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some simply prefer other paths. There are several.

**Prescription options.** Some non-hormonal medicines have evidence that they can reduce hot flashes. This applies to certain medicines originally developed for other conditions, and a newer group developed specifically against hot flashes. Each of them has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talk therapy and mind-body methods.** Cognitive behavioral therapy, adapted to the change of life, has evidence for making hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and for improving sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes many benefit from:**
- Clothes in layers that you can quickly take off
- A fan at the desk and at the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and dampening your personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help here)
- Regular physical activity and a regular sleep rhythm

**Supplements and natural remedies.** The evidence is mixed or limited for many of them, quality varies, and some interact with other medicine. Tell your doctor or the pharmacy about everything you take, also over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your own records before and during a change, and that is easier to judge than a feeling.

Most doctor appointments are short, and it is hard to remember a month of nights on the spot. You often remember the latest days or the worst. A simple log fills the gap.

**What a diary gives your doctor:**
- How often the symptoms come and how strong they are, not just that they come
- Whether it is getting better, worse or is unchanged
- What was going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medication
- A starting point to compare with if you try a treatment

**Make it easy.** A diary only helps if you keep it. MenoMap is built around a Wave button with one tap and an evening check with four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of records usually give a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Visit tab helps you choose questions and prints them together with your notes.

backTranslations.479:
Once you have gone 12 months without a period, **any bleeding from the vagina should be examined by a doctor**, even if it happened only once, and even if it was only spotting or pink or brown discharge.

In most cases the cause turns out not to be serious. Thinning of the lining of the vagina or uterus is, for example, common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a disease which is much easier to treat when it is discovered early. Therefore the public health recommendations say that you should get it examined rather than wait.

**If you receive hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns can be expected, depending on which type you take. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than normal or comes at the wrong time should also be examined.

**This is what to do:**
- Contact your doctor or the health service and say that you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Write down the date, how much it was and what else you have noticed. MenoMap can save it for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding occurred. The app reminds you to get it examined and includes it in your notes for the doctor's visit.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints in midlife, and it seldom has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly or make you too hot or damp to settle again.

**Other common contributing factors:**
- Having to pee at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but often gives a more restless second half of the night
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs or a partner who snores
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be signs of sleep apnea (worth bringing up, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What often helps.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layered clothes you can take off; a fixed time to get up; and less alcohol close to bedtime. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured and well-studied method, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What you can record.** For a week or two you can note your sleep score, night waves, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening check and the Wave log handle it with a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from Apple Health next to your night sweats, as context and not as an explanation.

**When to get checked.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example when you drive), your mood or your daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or gasping for air at night.
